knead.e: From Middle English kneden, from Old English cnedan, from Proto-West Germanic *knedan, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gnet- (“to press together”).
knead.g: To work and press into a mass, usually with the hands; especially, to work, as by repeated pressure with the knuckles, into a well mixed mas

kneading.e: From Middle English knedynge; equivalent to knead + -ing.
kneading.g: The process by which something is kneaded.

knee.e: From Middle English kne, from Old English cnēow, from Proto-West Germanic *kneu, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéw-o-m, a thematic derivative of *ǵónu. The obsolete plural kneen is from Middle English kneen, knen, kneon, kneuwene.
knee.g: In humans, the joint or the region of the joint in the middle part of the leg between the thigh and the shank.

knee-deep.e: From Middle English kne-depe; equivalent to knee + deep.

kneel.e: From Middle English knelen, from Old English cnēowlian (“to kneel”), equivalent to knee + -le.
kneel.g: To rest on one's bent knees, sometimes only one; to move to such a position.

knife.e: From Middle English knyf, knif, from late Old English cnīf, from Old Norse knífr or Proto-West Germanic *knīb, from Proto-Germanic *knībaz, from *knīpaną (“to pinch”), Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ- (compare Lithuanian gnýbti, žnýbti (“to pinch”), gnaibis (“pinching”)). The variant knive is first attested in 1733.
knife.g: A utensil or a tool designed for cutting, consisting of a flat piece of hard material, usually steel or other metal (the blade), usually sha

knit.e: From Middle English knytten, from Old English cnyttan, from Proto-West Germanic *knuttijan, from Proto-Germanic *knuttijaną, from *knuttô + *-janą.
knit.g: To turn thread or yarn into a piece of fabric by forming loops that are pulled through each other. This can be done by hand with needles or

knive.e: Knife (verb), which is now 150 times more common, is first attested in the 1860s.

knock.e: From Middle English knokken, from Old English cnocian, ġecnocian, ġecnucian, cnucian (“to knock, pound on, beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *knokōn, from Proto-Germanic *knukōną (“to knock”), a suffixed form of *knu-, *knew- (“to pound on, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gnew-, *gen- (“to squeeze, pinch, kink, ball up, concentrate”).
knock.g: An abrupt rapping sound, as from an impact of a hard object against wood.

knop.e: From Middle English knop, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch knoppe, from Proto-Germanic *knuppô, *knuppaz, *knappô, which is perhaps related to *knappō (“knob, boy”). Possible doublet of knave and knob.

knotted.e: From Middle English knotted, iknotted, from the past participle of the verb knotten.

know.e: From Middle English knowen, from Old English cnāwan (“to know, perceive, recognise”), from Proto-West Germanic *knāan, from Proto-Germanic *knēaną (“to know”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”). Remotely related also Dutch and German kennen, West Frisian kenne (see English ken).
know.g: To perceive the truth or factuality of; to be certain of; to be certain that.

know.e: Shortening of you know (sense 4)—Singapore English favours pro-drop constructions (Wee, 2003).
know.g: Used at the end of a sentence to draw attention to information one thinks the listener should keep in mind.

knowledge.e: From Middle English knowleche, knaweleche, cnawlece (“knowledge”), from knowen (“to know, recognise”) + -leche. For more on the Middle English suffix -leche, compare freelage.
knowledge.g: The fact of knowing about something; general understanding or familiarity with a subject, place, situation etc.

known.e: From Middle English knowen, from Old English cnāwen (past participle). Morphologically know + -n.
known.g: Identified as a specific type; famous, renowned.
